headline: Litton Das backs Tigers to win tri-series despite recent batting struggles
summary: Litton Das, the new ODI captain, believes Bangladesh can win the upcoming tri-nation series against Zimbabwe and Afghanistan, despite the team's recent struggles with batting, particularly away from home.
details: Litton Das, the new ODI captain, expressed optimism about Bangladesh's chances in the upcoming tri-nation series against Zimbabwe and Afghanistan. He stated, "If we play good cricket, why not?", when asked about the team's potential to become champions.

This confidence comes despite recent batting struggles, especially against the same two opponents. Bangladesh was whitewashed 3-0 by Afghanistan in October 2025 and lost 2-1 to Zimbabwe in July this year.

Litton emphasized the need for senior players to take responsibility and for the batting unit to ensure they bat out the full 50 overs. He noted the team's limited options with only six specialist batters.

The team's batting has crumbled away from home, particularly in the series against Zimbabwe and Afghanistan. In the Afghanistan series, Bangladesh failed to bat out 50 overs in any match, losing one by 200 runs.

Litton himself has shown improved form in 2026, scoring 300 runs in nine innings at an average of 42.86, including two half-centuries, after a dismal 2024-2025 period. He recently scored 53 and 102 in a Test against Afghanistan.

Bangladesh has batting depth on paper with players like Tanzid Tamim, Soumya Sarkar, Najmul Hossain Shanto, Towhid Hridoy, Mosaddek Hossain, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz. The bowling unit is considered a strength.

Zimbabwe also enters the series after a 3-0 loss to world champions Australia, though they pushed the world champions in one match. The tri-series opener for Bangladesh is against Zimbabwe in Abu Dhabi, a familiar venue where Bangladesh has won two of six ODIs.

headline: 90 dengue patients died and 28,820 hospitalised in first 16 days of October, raising concerns
summary: The escalating dengue outbreak has claimed 90 lives and led to nearly 29,000 hospitalisations in just over two weeks, highlighting a worsening public health crisis.
details: Bangladesh recorded 90 dengue patient deaths and 28,820 hospitalisations in the first 16 days of October alone. This alarming surge has intensified concerns about the country's worsening dengue outbreak.

According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), September saw 148 deaths and 43,774 hospitalisations. Earlier months also reported significant numbers: 43 deaths and 20,536 hospitalisations in August, 36 deaths and 9,206 hospitalisations in July, 13 deaths and 20,907 hospitalisations in June, and one death and 714 hospitalisations in May.

Health experts attribute the rising death toll to several critical factors. These include delayed hospitalisation, inadequate early diagnosis, the absence of an effective three-tier dengue management system, and a general increase in infection rates.

A recent death review conducted by the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR) revealed concerning statistics. More than one-third of the 119 reviewed patients died within a day of hospital admission, indicating rapid deterioration.

The review further found that 62.5 percent of deaths were due to dengue shock syndrome, 31.2 percent from expanded dengue syndrome, and 16.1 percent from dengue with bleeding. Additionally, many patients experienced diagnostic delays of at least three days, exacerbating their conditions.

Medicine specialist Dr ABM Abdullah highlighted that repeated infections and delays in both diagnosis and treatment are major contributors to dengue fatalities. Patients infected multiple times face a higher risk of developing severe complications.

Prof Abdullah urged the public, especially children and individuals with underlying health conditions like diabetes or heart disease, not to ignore even mild symptoms. He advised seeking medical advice and testing for symptoms such as fever, body aches, vomiting, or sore throat, and warned against self-medication with painkillers.

Prof HM Nazmul Ahsan, from Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital, expressed concern over inconsistent application of national dengue treatment guidelines. He stressed that treatment should be based on a patient's clinical condition, not solely on low platelet counts.

Prof Nazmul warned that unnecessary platelet transfusions, inappropriate fluid administration, and excessive fluid loading can lead to complications and even death. He also called for improved access to dengue testing, particularly for low-income communities in both urban and rural areas.

Public health expert Mushtuq Husain advocated for a three-tier dengue management system to reduce deaths and alleviate pressure on major hospitals. This system would involve primary, secondary, and tertiary healthcare facilities working in coordination.

Under this proposed system, primary healthcare facilities would offer free or low-cost dengue detection and initial testing. Patients needing closer monitoring would be referred to upazila health complexes and district hospitals, while medical colleges and specialised hospitals would handle severe cases.

An entomologist at Jahangirnagar University, Prof Kabirul Bashar, predicted a slight decline in dengue cases in November. However, he cautioned that a significant reduction is unlikely before December, citing a forecasting model that suggests cases could continue rising for up to six weeks after the last rainfall.
